passages.t: Is there no God in Israel?
passages.happening:
‘After the death of Ahab, Moab rebelled against Israel’ (verse 1). Ahab's son Ahaziah falls through the lattice of his upper room in Samaria and is badly hurt. He sends messengers: “Go inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will recover from this injury” (verse 2).

The angel of the LORD sends Elijah to meet them on the road with a question, ‘Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are on your way to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?’ (verse 3). And a verdict: the king will not get up from his bed. He will die (verse 4).

The messengers turn back and repeat it all to the king. He asks what the man looked like. “He was a hairy man,” they answer, “with a leather belt around his waist” (verse 8). The king knows at once. “It was Elijah the Tishbite” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Second Kings opens without a break from 1 Kings, which ended with Ahaziah on the throne, walking in his parents' ways and serving Baal. This chapter shows what that means in practice. When the king is in trouble, he turns to a foreign god. He reigned only briefly, about 853 to 852 BC.

Ancient kings routinely sought oracles about illness, and a god with a name for healing might draw inquirers from far away. Ahaziah does not ask the LORD, or even a Baal in Samaria. He sends to a Philistine shrine. Ekron was one of the five chief Philistine cities, on the coastal plain west of Judah, and an inscription naming the city was found at its site, Tel Miqne, in 1996. The name Baal-zebub means lord of flies. Many scholars think it is an Israelite mockery of the title Baal-zebul, Baal the prince; others think it was a real local god who guarded against flies and the disease they carried.

The word for inquire, darash, is the ordinary word for seeking a god's guidance, and it comes five times in the chapter. The question is where a person goes for a word when life is threatened.

The note that Moab rebelled is left hanging until chapter 3. Moab, east of the Dead Sea, had been subject to Israel since Omri's day. The Mesha Stele, a Moabite king's inscription found at Dhiban in 1868, gives Moab's own account of breaking free.

Elijah's hairy garment and leather belt were the dress of someone outside the court and its comforts. It was enough for the king to know exactly who had met his men.
passages.later: Matthew describes John the Baptist in the same way: ‘John wore a garment of camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist’ (Matthew 3:4). The New Testament names John as the one who came ‘in the spirit and power of Elijah’ (Luke 1:17). And Jesus' opponents used a form of the same god's name, Beelzebul, for the prince of demons (Matthew 12:24).
passages.asks: When Ahaziah was hurt, he looked for help everywhere except to the LORD. Ask where you turn first when your life or health is threatened. And ask what that shows about whom you really trust.

passages.t: Three captains, and a king who died
passages.happening:
King Ahaziah sends a captain with fifty men. They find Elijah sitting on top of a hill, and the captain orders the man of God, in the king's name, to come down (verse 9). Elijah answers, “If I am a man of God, may fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men” (verse 10). Fire comes down and consumes them. A second captain comes with fifty men and the same order, made more urgent, and the same thing happens (verses 11-12).

The third captain goes up and falls on his knees. He begs, “Man of God, may my life and the lives of these fifty servants please be precious in your sight” (verse 13). The angel of the LORD tells Elijah, “Go down with him. Do not be afraid of him” (verse 15).

Elijah goes down and says to the king's face what he had said on the road: he will not get up from his bed (verse 16). ‘So Ahaziah died according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken’ (verse 17). He has no son, and his brother Jehoram succeeds him.
passages.hearers:
Companies of fifty were ordinary units in an ancient Israelite army. To send armed men to summon a prophet was to claim that the king's command outranked the word of God, and that is exactly the claim the chapter tests.

The chapter is built on threes. The LORD's question is spoken three times, by the angel, by the messengers and by Elijah. Three captains come. The first two give orders, and Elijah answers with a play on words: if he is a man of God, ish elohim, let the fire of God, esh elohim, come down. Fire had answered Elijah on Mount Carmel, and it will appear again in the chariot of fire in the next chapter. The third captain comes on his knees, and the pattern breaks.

Movement up and down carries the story. The king will not come down from his bed, the captains order the man of God to come down, fire comes down from heaven, and at last Elijah goes down with the third captain, by the LORD's word and not the king's.

Verse 17 dates Jehoram of Israel's accession by Jehoram of Judah's second year, and 3:1 dates it by Jehoshaphat's eighteenth year. The usual explanation is that Jehoshaphat's son shared the throne with his father for some years, so the same moment could be dated by either king. Both kingdoms had a king named Jehoram, or Joram, at the same time.
passages.later: When a Samaritan village would not receive Jesus, James and John asked, “Lord, do You want us to call down fire from heaven to consume them?” (Luke 9:54). ‘But Jesus turned and rebuked them’ (Luke 9:55).
passages.hard:
Why did a hundred soldiers die by fire for obeying their king's orders?

The deaths of the first two companies are troubling, and readers have long felt it. The text itself gives some help. The first two captains come not to ask but to command the man of God to come down, in the name of a king who has just rejected the LORD, and the second adds urgency to the order. The chapter presents their approach as the king's assault on the LORD's messenger, and the fire answers that challenge as fire answered the prophets of Baal on Carmel. The third captain shows that another way was open: he humbles himself and is spared.

Still, the soldiers were not the ones who sent to Ekron. Some interpreters stress that in the Old Testament the treatment of God's messenger counts as the treatment of God himself, and that this was a decisive moment in the struggle with the worship of Baal. Others stress that the New Testament deliberately refuses this model, since Jesus rebuked the disciples who wanted to repeat Elijah's fire. Both readings agree that the chapter is not a pattern for believers to follow. It gives no one a warrant to wish harm, or to call down judgment, on those who oppose them.
passages.asks: The third captain came with a request, not a command, and was spared. Ask whether you come to God to demand or to ask. And ask how you hold together a God who judges and a Savior who refused to destroy the village that turned him away.
